# Vaṅgīsa Saṁyutta (SN 8)

**ID:** SN 8  
**Section:** Saṁyuttanikāya (sn)  
**Collection:** Sutta  
**Title (Pali):** Vaṅgīsa Saṁyutta  
**tipitaka.org (CST):** [https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0301m.mul7.xml](https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0301m.mul7.xml)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Vaṅgīsa Saṁyutta* (SN 8) is the eighth section of the *Saṁyuttanikāya*, situated within the *Sagāthavagga* [Bodhi 2003; von Hinüber 1996]. It comprises 12 discourses (SN 8.1–8.12) framed around verses spoken by the venerable Vaṅgīsa, whom the Buddha declared the foremost of his disciples gifted with inspirational, impromptu speech (*paṭibhānavantānaṁ*, AN I 24) [Bodhi 2003]. Renowned for his literary sophistication and spontaneous verse compositions, Vaṅgīsa's poems candidly portray his early struggles as a newly ordained monk fighting sexual attraction and discontent (*arati*), as well as his joyful devotion praising the Buddha and senior disciples such as Sāriputta, Moggallāna, and Aññā Koṇḍañña [Bodhi 2003; Hazra 1994].

Within Pali literature, the verses of the *Vaṅgīsa Saṁyutta* closely correspond to the 71 verses constituting the *Vaṅgīsattheragāthā* (Thag 1209–1279), the longest chapter in the *Theragāthā*, though the *Theragāthā* recension lacks the prose narrative settings found in the *Saṁyuttanikāya* [Bodhi 2003; von Hinüber 1996].

The seventh discourse (*Pavāraṇāsutta*, SN 8.7)—which celebrates the formal end of the rains retreat and presents the Buddha as a skilled physician who destroys the dart of craving [Buddhist Philosophy and Meditation Practice 2012]—possesses especially extensive cross-canonical parallels. Notably, the *Madhyamāgama* parallel contains an expanded preamble describing the Buddha as the unsurpassed "Medicine-King" [Radich 2007].

- [Hazra 1994] Kanai Lal Hazra, Pāli Language and Literature (1994) — Summarized the narrative themes concerning Vaṅgīsa's overcome discontent and passions.
